analysis.one_liner: Waves FDA registration fees for small medical device makers and charges foreign companies eight times more.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced July 20, 2026, has no cosponsors and sits in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill changes how the FDA charges its annual registration fee for medical device establishments. Companies with fewer than 20 full-time employees would get their fee waived entirely for three years, then half off for two more, and the FDA could no longer deny a waiver based on past unpaid fees. Foreign-owned companies would be barred from the waiver and would pay eight times the standard fee. The changes would take effect 90 days after any enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: Small U.S. medical device makers — those with fewer than 20 full-time employees, counting affiliates — gain the most: a full fee waiver for three years and a 50% discount for the next two. Foreign-owned companies gain nothing; they are excluded from the waiver and would pay 8x the standard registration fee. Larger U.S. device makers are largely unaffected directly, though they may indirectly shoulder more of the FDA's user-fee funding burden.

how_it_helps.text: Qualifying small businesses (under 20 full-time employees including affiliates) would pay 0% of the annual establishment registration fee for three years and 50% for the following two years [S2].
The FDA could not deny a waiver because the establishment failed to pay the fee in earlier years, removing a prior-payment hurdle [S2].

Applicants would use Small Business Administration size and affiliation standards and submit a recent tax return or payroll register to prove size, giving clearer, more objective qualification rules [S2].
Foreign-organized entities could not apply for the waiver or form a U.S. entity for that purpose, aiming the relief at domestic small firms [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign-owned device establishments would pay eight times the standard registration fee, a cost that could be passed into device prices. Because FDA device review is largely funded by industry user fees, waiving fees for small firms shifts a modest portion of the funding load onto other fee-paying companies, and reduced fee revenue could marginally affect FDA device-review capacity if not offset elsewhere.
analysis.who_pays_short: Foreign device companies and the FDA fee pool

drawbacks.text: Foreign companies would face an 8x registration fee, a cost likely to be passed on to buyers of devices and potentially to reduce foreign competition in the U.S. market [S2].
Waiving fees shrinks the user-fee revenue the FDA counts on for device review; unless offset elsewhere, that could modestly slow device reviews that patients wait on [S2].
Eligibility expires after five years of coverage, so the relief is temporary for any given firm, and a company the Secretary determines is not a small business loses eligibility permanently [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real but narrow: it lowers a compliance cost for very small device firms, which can matter for startups. The offsetting 8x fee on foreign companies raises costs in the device supply chain and may be passed to buyers, and waived fees modestly drain FDA's device-review funding. On balance it is a small-business relief bill with modest side costs rather than a major consumer measure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no further action while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the bill in the House on July 20, 2026 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds the bill as Congress continues its session [S4].
No other members have cosponsored the bill [S3].
No committee action, floor vote, or Senate action appears in the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet — the bill is dormant in committee, so current fee rules still apply and no company or consumer has been affected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — bill dormant in committee

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 20, 2026 and sent it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no cosponsors have signed on, so the partisan shape of support or opposition is not yet visible [S3].

industries.note: Firms with fewer than 20 employees would pay nothing for three years and half price for two more on their FDA annual registration fee, easing a fixed compliance cost for small startups. Consumers benefit only indirectly, if at all, through the survival of small suppliers.

They are barred from the waiver and would pay eight times the standard registration fee. That cost would likely flow into device prices or reduce foreign competitors' U.S. presence, which could mean fewer options for patients.

industries.industry: Larger U.S. device manufacturers and the FDA device user-fee pool
industries.note: Waived small-business fees shrink the user-fee revenue FDA relies on for device reviews; the shortfall, if not offset, spreads across remaining fee payers and can marginally affect review speed that patients depend on.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since referral, the bill faces the fate of most first-term House bills: it is likely to die quietly in committee unless the sponsor actively pushes for a hearing or attaches it to a larger FDA user-fee reauthorization package.
